facts.statement: Safe driving depends on clear sight, alertness, freedom from alcohol or drug impairment, health and emotional readiness.
Poor vision makes it harder to detect road conditions and respond to danger promptly.
Kansas requires a successful vision test before issuing a driver license.
The vision standard is at least 20/40 in one eye, using corrective lenses if needed.
A corrective-lens license restriction requires the driver to wear glasses or contacts while driving.
Get regular eye examinations because deteriorating vision may otherwise go unnoticed.
A corrective-lens requirement applies even to a short local drive.
Keep spare corrective lenses in the vehicle in case the usual pair is damaged or lost.
Avoid tinted lenses at night because they reduce the light available for seeing.
Horns, sirens and skidding-tire sounds can warn a driver about danger.
A change in tire noise may signal a changed road surface or tire condition.
Engine sounds can provide clues about how the engine is operating.
Hearing loss can develop gradually without being noticed.
Fatigue is physical or mental tiredness caused by factors such as strain, repetition, illness or insufficient sleep.
Fatigue weakens vision and judgment.
Fatigue can distort judgments about speed and distance.
A fatigued driver may take longer to decide and become irritated more easily.
Fatigue increases crash risk and may lead to falling asleep while driving.
Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep to stay properly alert during the day.
On a long trip, plan a rest break about every 100 miles or every 2 hours.
A travel companion can provide conversation and share driving duties.
Before a trip, avoid alcohol and medicines that cause sedation.
Check medicine labels or ask a doctor about sedating effects before driving.
Needing loud radio sound or an open window to remain awake is a fatigue warning.
Trouble keeping the eyes open is a fatigue warning.
Drifting out of the lane is a fatigue warning.
When fatigued, stop driving and use an exit, rest area or overnight sleeping place.
The handbook recommends a 15-to-20-minute nap in a safe parking place when sleepy.
The handbook says caffeine comparable to 2 cups of coffee can temporarily improve alertness.
Caffeine wears off and must not be relied on to prevent fatigue.
The handbook suggests having caffeine, followed by a brief nap, to gain benefits from both.
Try to avoid late-night driving between midnight and 6 a.m.
Sleep is the best prevention for fatigue.
A distraction is anything that draws attention away from operating the vehicle.
A mental distraction can be dangerous even while the driver's eyes face the road.
Using a phone, navigation system or other electronic device can distract a driver.
Changing audio or climate settings while moving can distract a driver.
Grooming, eating, drinking or smoking can divert driving attention.
Conversations and attending to children or pets can distract a driver.
Reading maps or other material can distract a driver.
Reaching for a dropped object can distract a driver.
Watching a roadside crash or traffic stop can divert attention from driving.
Sunlight or a sunset can become an outside distraction.
People or objects in the roadway, as well as road construction, can divert attention from driving.
Reading billboards or roadside advertisements can distract a driver.
Park safely before using a cell phone.
Avoid arguments and stressful conversations that compete with attention to the road.
Allow time to stop for food instead of eating while driving.
Secure children properly and give them suitable activities before traveling.
Secure pets in a carrier or portable kennel before moving the vehicle.
Set vehicle controls before departure, at normal stops or with a passenger's help.
Keep attention on the immediate travel path rather than distant distractions.
Plan the route and review maps before driving.
If a map must be checked during a trip, first park in a safe place.
Do not converse with friends in another vehicle while driving.
Do not wear music headphones while driving.
The driver remains responsible for safe vehicle operation when a distraction contributes to a crash.
The handbook advises avoiding excessive caffeine when responding to fatigue.
